extracted.intended_audience: readers seeking guidance on social etiquette and polite behaviour (historical/gentlemanly conduct)
extracted.subtask_description: A prescriptive set of rules for polite social behaviour (gestures, speech, dress, deference, visiting, writing, and conduct in company), drawn from a historical etiquette manual. Each criterion states a particular manner or prohibition and gives explanatory guidance and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16th. Do not puff up the Cheeks, Loll not out the tongue rub the Hands, or beard, thrust out the lips, or bite them or keep the lips too open or too close
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid vulgar or exaggerated facial and hand gestures (puffing cheeks, sticking out the tongue, fiddling with beard or hands, thrusting or biting lips, keeping lips too open or too tight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is very low to puff out the cheeks, to put out the tongue, to pull one's beard, rub one's hands, poke out or bite the lips, or to keep them too tightly closed or too open. (French: C'est une vilainie...) These actions mark bad manners and should be avoided in polite company.

rubrics_metrics.name: 17th. Be no Flatterer, neither Play with any that delights not to be Play'd Withal
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not flatter people with insincere praise or play practical jokes on those who dislike them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not wheedle or gain people by 'honied words'—flattery shows lack of esteem and implies the other is easily tricked. Also avoid joking or teasing those who take offense; do not use mockery or praises before you have genuine regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18th. Read no Letters, Books, or Papers in Company but when there is a Necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not read books, letters, or papers in ordinary conversation unless necessary and with permission; do not handle or comment on others' writings without being asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading during conversation is directly opposed to politeness except in pressing matters or briefly—and even then ask leave unless you are the senior. Do not handle others' books or approach them to view without permission, nor praise or criticize them before being asked; avoid crowding someone reading their letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: 19th. let your Countenance be pleasant but in Serious Matters Somewhat grave
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a composed, open, and tranquil facial expression; avoid being excessively ecstatic in serious matters or affectively solemn in ordinary conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The face should not look fantastic, changeable, absent, rapt, or covered with sadness; it should be open and tranquil. Do not be overly joyous in serious affairs nor affect an unnatural gravity in familiar conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20th. The Gestures of the Body must be Suited to the discourse you are upon
rubrics_metrics.description: Match bodily gestures to the subject matter of your speech; avoid excessive or awkward gesticulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let gestures be agreeable to your discourse; e.g., it's improper to point to the earth while speaking of heaven. (Maxim: assume an elegant posture while speaking.) Avoid excessive and awkward movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 21st. Reproach none for the Infirmaties of Nature, nor Delight to Put them that have in mind thereof
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reproach or take pleasure in exposing others' natural infirmities; avoid words that shame people for things beyond their control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reproaching anyone for defects, even natural ones, and do not delight in uttering words that cause shame. Hawkins adds these are defects 'which by no Art can be amended'—do not mock them.

rubrics_metrics.name: 22d. Shew not yourself glad at the Misfortune of another though he were your enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Never show joy at another's misfortune (even an enemy's), as it indicates malice and a desire to see harm done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing gladness at others' misfortunes argues a mischievous mind and suggests you would have acted if you had power. French text echoes this as rude and indicative of ill will.

rubrics_metrics.name: 23d. When you see a Crime punished, you may be inwardly Pleased; but always shew Pity to the Suffering Offender
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to be inwardly satisfied when justice is done, but publicly show pity and consider moral failings as cautionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may inwardly take delight in vigilance that punishes offenders for public quiet, yet show pity to the offender and see their lack of morality as a warning to yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: 24th. Do not laugh too loud or too much at any Publick spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive or loud laughter at public spectacles to prevent making yourself the object of ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laugh not too much or too loudly in public spectacles; overdoing it may make you appear the only thing worthy to be laughed at.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25th. Superfluous Complements and all Affectation of Ceremony are to be avoided, yet where due they are not to be Neglected
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid affected civility and unnecessary ceremony, but faithfully observe necessary and advantageous forms of politeness that prevent offending others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While one should not practice affected civility, be exact in observing what is necessary and useful to show good upbringing and what cannot be omitted without shocking companions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 26th. In pulling off your Hat to Persons of Distinction... make a Reverence, bowing more or less according to the Custom
rubrics_metrics.description: When uncovering before persons of distinction (nobles, magistrates, clergy), hold hat in hand and make an appropriate bow according to their dignity and local custom; avoid uncovering when inappropriate or making it an affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show respect hat in hand, holding the inside toward you, and incline the body as dignity and custom demand. Not uncovering before those deserving respect is rude; uncovering when not fitting is affected. In saluting by words, use the usual compliment polite people use.

rubrics_metrics.name: 27th. Tis ill manners to bid one more eminent than yourself be covered as well as not to do it to whom it's due...
rubrics_metrics.description: It is rude to ask a superior to remain covered or to fail to ask a superior to uncover; do not be hasty to put on your hat in the presence of those of quality, and observe proper order in seating and ceremonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asking a superior to be covered or failing to do proper uncovering is uncivil. If urged once or twice, it is permissible to cover, unless local usage forbids it. Among equals or with older persons, grant the request promptly. Excessive ceremony and compliments are tiresome; the same rules extend to taking places and sitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: 28th. If any one come to Speak to you while you are Sitting Stand up tho he be your Inferiour...
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand when someone comes to speak to you even if they are inferior, except when on very intimate terms; when hosting, seat guests according to station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are sitting when someone visits, rise as they approach if their dignity demands it, whether equal or inferior (but not if very familiar). If at home with seats to offer, arrange to treat each guest according to his merit or station.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29th. When you meet with one of Greater Quality than yourself, Stop, and retire especially if it be at a Door or any Straight place to give way for him to Pass
rubrics_metrics.description: When encountering someone of superior rank, pause or step aside—retreat to a doorway or street corner—to give them passage, beyond ordinary salutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stop a little, retreat to an entrance or corner to make way for those deserving special respect; Walker adds in narrow ways press to make more room.

rubrics_metrics.name: 30th. In walking the highest Place in most Countrys Seems to be on the right hand therefore Place yourself on the left of him whom you desire to Honour...
rubrics_metrics.description: Yield the place of honor when walking together: commonly the right or the middle (for three), and when beside a wall yield the side that custom designates to the worthiest person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give companions the place of honour pointed out by usage—often the right is a mark of esteem. With three, the highest quality takes the middle. In France, when walking by a wall, the place near the wall is left to the most qualified.

rubrics_metrics.name: 31st. If any one far Surpasses others, either in age Estate, or Merit would give Place to a meaner than himself...
rubrics_metrics.description: A superior who yields place to an inferior should not press the inferior repeatedly to accept, and the inferior should not assume worthiness; repeated insistence can embarrass or reduce esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a much older or higher person wishes to honour an inferior, that inferior should not presume himself worthy; the superior must not press too much or show deference beyond once or twice lest persistent entreaty lower the good opinion or cause an incivility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 32d. To one that is your equal, or not much inferior you are to give the chief Place in your Lodging and he to who 'tis offered ought at the first to refuse it but at the Second to accept though not without acknowledging his own unworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Among equals, give the most honourable place to a guest; the guest should initially refuse but accept upon a second insistence while modestly acknowledging unworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When receiving someone into your home, give the most honourable seat. The person offered it should first refuse, but upon a second request should obey. Acceptance of the first place should be accompanied by acknowledgement of unworthiness (modest behaviour).

rubrics_metrics.name: 33d. They that are in Dignity or in office have in all places Preceedency but whilst they are Young they ought to respect those that are their equals in Birth or other Qualitys
rubrics_metrics.description: Those in command or office are given precedence, but if they are young they should respect equals in birth, age, or academic degree and modestly return offers of highest place before accepting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First place is given to those in command or judicial charge. Young holders of such positions ought to respect those of equal noble birth, those much older, or those with doctorates, even if they hold no public office; they should first return an offer of the highest place and then accept it modestly as a favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: 34th. It is good Manners to prefer them to whom we speak before ourselves especially if they be above us with whom in no Sort we ought to begin
rubrics_metrics.description: Always speak better of your interlocutors than of yourself, and never dispute with those of superior rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is the height of politeness to speak favorably of those you converse with rather than yourself, especially when they are of superior rank—do not contest with them in any manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35th. Let your Discourse with Men of Business be Short and Comprehensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep conversation with busy men brief and to the point; avoid florid compliments and rely more on clear looks or concise speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time, place, age, and differences should regulate compliments. With men of business, cut matters short and spare them fine compliments; make yourself understood more by looks than excessive words.

rubrics_metrics.name: 36th. Artificers & Persons of low Degree ought not to use many ceremonies to Lords... and those of high Degree ought to treat them with affibility & Courtesie, without Arrogancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower-status persons should show respect (not excessive ceremony) to the high-born; the nobility should treat artisans and the lower orders gently and avoid arrogance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined politeness should not overly burden artisans and common people regarding nobles and magistrates; it is reasonable to honor them, and likewise the nobility should spare and avoid all kinds of pride when treating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37th. In Speaking to men of Quality do not lean nor Look them full in the Face, nor approach too near them at lest Keep a full Pace from them
rubrics_metrics.description: When speaking to persons of quality, do not lean on objects, stare up at their faces, or approach too close—keep about a full step's distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prop your body; do not raise your eyes to their face; do not approach too near—maintain a full pace of distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 38th. In visiting the Sick, do not Presently play the Physicion if you be not Knowing therein
rubrics_metrics.description: When visiting the sick, do not attempt to act as a physician unless you are experienced in medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not immediately play the physician if you lack experience in that science—avoid offering medical treatment or advice beyond your competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 39th. In writing or Speaking, give to every Person his due Title According to his Degree & the Custom of the Place
rubrics_metrics.description: Address people by the appropriate title in speech and letters, following local custom and the person's rank; when writing, proofread, sand the writing if needed, and avoid folding paper before ink dries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulate address by country custom and degree of dignity. Read over letters to correct mistakes, sand writing when necessary, and never fold paper until letters are dry lest they be effaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: 40th. Strive not with your Superiers in argument, but always Submit your Judgment to others with Modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not argue with superiors; modestly defer to their more mature judgment, recognizing the greater likelihood of error in youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit your opinion to the riper judgment of superiors with modesty; since the possibility of error accompanies green rather than gray hairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 41st. Undertake not to teach your equal in the art himself Professes; it flavours of arrogancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not presumptuously try to teach a person your equal in the same profession or art, as it shows arrogance and rashness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting to instruct an equal in the art he practices; it savours of arrogance and will mark your judgment as rash. Walker echoes caution in discoursing about a person's own faculty except by asking questions and seeming to learn.

rubrics_metrics.name: 42d. Let your ceremonies in curtesie be proper to the Dignity of his place
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor courtesy and ceremonious behaviour to the dignity and station of the person you address; extravagant honors to low-born persons are absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courtesy should be appropriate to the rank of the addressee—do not honour a clown with courtly words of magnificence; match ceremonies to dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 43d. Do not express Joy before one sick or in pain for that contrary Passion will aggravate his Misery
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid expressing joy in the presence of the sick or suffering since contrary emotions may worsen their distress; instead, sympathize to provide relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not express joy before a sick or pained person; sympathize with their infirmities, which affords grateful easement by seeming participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 44th. When a man does all he can though it Succeeds not well blame not him that did it
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not blame someone who has done their utmost to advance your affairs even if they failed; they deserve praise rather than reproach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One who has done all possible to further your business, though not achieving the hoped success, should not be reproached—he is more worthy of praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: 45th. Being to advise or reprehend any one, consider whether it ought to be in publick or in Private... and in reproving Shew no signs of Cholar but do it with all Sweetness and Mildness
rubrics_metrics.description: When advising or reproving, consider timing, place (public vs private), appropriate wording, and avoid anger—reprimand with moderation, sweetness, and mildness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide if rebuke is better private or public, now or later, and choose words carefully—especially for those already reprimanded. Avoid anger; act with moderation and gentleness when giving advice or reprimand.

rubrics_metrics.name: 46th. Take all Admonitions thankfully in what Time or Place Soever given but afterwards... let him know it that gave them
rubrics_metrics.description: Receive admonitions graciously wherever given; if you are innocent, later choose a convenient time/place to demonstrate or explain your innocence—prefer to show truth and relieve the admonisher over defending by excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hear rebukes with goodwill and gratitude. Afterward, if innocent and it is appropriate to prove it, pick a proper time to show the truth and relieve the other's anxiety—more to make him see the truth than to excuse yourself, especially if you are under his charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47th. Mock not nor Jest at anything of Importance... if you Deliver anything witty and Pleasent abtain from Laughing thereat yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mocking important or shameful matters; if you deliver a witty remark, refrain from laughing at it yourself—keep repartee tasteful and non-malicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not amuse yourself with equivocation about important or shameful things. If you jest, avoid biting or tearing like a dog; witticisms should be apt and elegant without exciting indignation. Do not let pleasantries degenerate into buffoonery or indecency; if you make others laugh, try not to laugh yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48th. Wherein wherein you reprove Another be unblameable yourself; for example is is more prevalent than Precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: When reproving someone, be beyond reproach yourself—set an example because actions carry more weight than words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your own conduct is virtuous in the point you wish to preserve in another; example is more effective than precept and ratifies advice by serious prosecution of the virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49th. Use no Reproachfull Language against any one neither Curse nor Revile
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use reproachful language, curses, or revilings against anyone; such imprecations reveal your passions rather than harm the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reproachful speech, curses, or revilings—the utterance betrays your emotions and does little to hurt the person addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50th. Be not hasty to believe flying Reports to the Disparagement of any
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not quickly believe rumors that disparage someone; let charity guide judgment until certainty is obtained to protect reputation and avoid rashness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not too suddenly believe a flying rumour of a friend or another; let charity guide your judgment until more certainty—this secures reputation and frees you from rashness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51st. Wear not your Cloths, foul, unript or Dusty but See they be Brush'd once every day at least and take heed that you approach not to any Uncleanness
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep clothes clean, mended, and brushed daily; avoid sitting or kneeling in filthy places and fold garments neatly when removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow clothes to remain dirty, torn, dusty, or threadbare—have them brushed at least once a day. Take care where you sit, kneel, or rest elbows; do not carry cloak over arm in swaggering fashion. Fold coats/cloaks neatly and mind where you place them.

rubrics_metrics.name: 52nd. In your Apparel be Modest and endeavour to accomodate Nature, rather than to procure Admiration keep to the Fashion of your equals Such as are Civil and orderly with respect to Times and Places
rubrics_metrics.description: Dress modestly and in accordance with natural shape and the restrained fashion of your equals; prioritize simplicity over ostentation and consider time and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose clothes like those of companions considered genteel and moderate, considering time and place with discretion. Aim to be the most simply and modestly dressed of your equals rather than affect the finest raiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 53d. Run not in the Streets, neither go too slowly nor with Mouth open... Walk not upon the toes, nor in a Dancing or skipping manner... Strike not the heels together, nor stoop when there is no occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an appropriate, steady gait: do not run, dawdle, walk with mouth open, shuffle, stamp, walk on toes, dance-step, stoop unnecessarily, or make inappropriate foot gestures (e.g., striking heels together in church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against hurried steps, gaping mouth, excessive body movement, stooping, dangling hands, or shaking arms; do not pull up stockings in the street, walk on toes, skip like dancing, stoop or lower the head, advance with measured steps, strike heels on entering church, or leave bareheaded unless devotion requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54th. Play not the Peacock, looking everywhere about you, to See if you be well Deck't...
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid vainly preening yourself in public (checking dress, shoes, stockings) or displaying affectations (pen in mouth/ear, flowers in hat); keep handkerchief hidden and clean before offering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not strut like a peacock checking your attire. Do not leave your room with pen in mouth or behind ear, or put flowers in ear/bonnet/hat. Do not hold or display pocket-handkerchief in obtrusive ways—keep it hidden but accessible; never present it unless clean or hardly unfolded.

rubrics_metrics.name: 55th. Eat not in the Streets, nor in ye House, out of Season
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not eat while walking in streets or eat at untimely moments in the house—at least abstain from eating in presence of others out of meal times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never walk eating in roads, alone or in company, especially in a crowd. Do not begin to eat in the house out of meal-times; at least abstain in presence of others.
